author: Al Jazeera English
description:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded to American scientist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for pioneering work in optogenetics, a technique that uses light to control nerve-cell activity and has transformed scientists' understanding of how the brain works. Hegemann and Nagel's research into light-sensitive proteins in algae helped lay the foundations for the technique, which Deisseroth later combined with nerve cells to allow researchers to switch individual neurons on or off and study their role in behaviours including learning, fear, memory and movement. The Nobel Committee described the discovery as a new era in neuroscience, while researchers are also exploring potential medical applications, including treatments for some forms of blindness and more precise stimulation for cochlear implants. The three laureates will share a prize of 12 million Swedish crowns, about $1.2m. 

Al Jazeera's Paul Rhys, reporting from Stock
title: Nobel medicine prize honours three scientists for breakthrough in optogenetics

description:
The United States has withdrawn all its bombers from RAF Fairford in the UK after several men were arrested on suspicion of planning ‘terrorist acts’ near the base. The men were later released on bail, and a legal expert said that if counter-terrorism police believed they posed such a threat, they would still be in custody. The base hosted American B-52 and B-1 bombers, which the US used to strike Iran during the war. The warplanes have been moved back to the US after Washington decided it was not secure enough to keep them at Fairford. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said RAF Fairford is safe, but the base has fallen quiet, with no US bombers present. The relocation could make President Donald Trump's Operation Epic Fury against Iran more logistically complicated, as RAF Fairford is about 4,000km closer to Iran than the bombers' US home bases. 

Al Jazeera’s Camille Nedelec reports from RAF Fairford airbase in the UK.

The ⁠military operation by the internationally recognised government of Yemen to retake ⁠⁠territory held by ⁠⁠the Houthis will be long and difficult, a defence analyst says.

“All signs are pointing towards a long battle,” said Baraa Shiban, associate fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute.

“We might be witnessing yet another round of years of conflict inside Yemen. And, unfortunately, it’s the Yemeni public who are going to bear the brunt of this escalation,” he told Al Jazeera from Istanbul.

While some suggest the operation will wrap up quickly, Shiban said the reality is otherwise. “I don’t think it’s going to be an easy and quick operation. We might be looking into years.”

The already long-running conflict also points towards a failure of the international community, which despite a ceasefire in 2022 has been unable to achieve any breakthrough towards a lasting peace, he added.

description:
When leaders of the United States insist that the US-Israel war on Iran is about nuclear weapons and not about oil, Iran’s leaders don’t believe them, former Iranian diplomat Hossein Mousavian argues.

Mousavian and former US diplomat Alan Eyre - both of whom were involved in previous negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme - tell host Steve Clemons that the conflict is not heading to a peace deal or even “permanent stalemate” anytime soon.

US President Donald Trump's administration prefers quick wins to diplomacy, Eyre argued, “and the responsibility is on the countries in the region to take more of a lead … with US buy-in, not US leadership.”
